summary: Describes an architecture for a global, scalable and distributed system that maps a geographic location to a URL, using the LoST protocol. It draws on hierarchical lookup ideas similar to DNS. Emergency services are an example of where such lookups matter.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 5582 describes how a device can find the address of a service that depends on its location. A set of cooperating lookup servers directs the request to the organization responsible for that area.

subtitle: A distributed lookup system that directs a location and service request to the right service address.

tldr.problem: A service may be provided by different local organizations, and the right provider can depend on a person's location.
tldr.mechanism: LoST clients ask resolvers, which use forest guides to find a tree of authoritative mapping servers. The tree narrows the location to a service URI.
tldr.outcome: The design distributes mapping data among independent operators and can also return local service numbers. RFC 5582 is Informational and does not define a new protocol.

today: RFC 5582 is an Informational RFC published in September 2009. The unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it; the document describes an architecture using LoST rather than defining a new protocol.

sections.title: The Location-to-Service Mapping Problem
sections.content:
Some services are provided locally, so a person's location helps determine which provider should receive a request. Emergency calls are one example: the caller's physical location helps select the appropriate public safety answering point (PSAP). The same general mapping problem can apply to food delivery, directory services, and roadside assistance.

The system maps a geographic or civic location and a service identifier to one or more service URIs. A service URI is an address that lets an Internet system contact a service provider. RFC 5582 describes an architecture using the Location-to-Service Translation (LoST) protocol, specified in RFC 5222.
sections.plainLanguage: The device needs a service address that fits the place where the person is. The system finds that address without requiring the person to know which local organization provides the service.

sections.title: Four Roles in the Lookup System
sections.content:
The architecture separates four logical roles. A seeker is a LoST client that asks for a mapping. A resolver receives the seeker's request, can cache earlier results, and knows one or more forest guides. A forest guide tracks the geographic coverage of trees for a service. A tree is a hierarchy of authoritative mapping servers (AMSs) that hold the mapping information.

A tree can be run across administrative boundaries, and its nodes can be replicated as a cluster to share load and provide redundancy. A forest guide points a resolver or seeker toward the appropriate tree; the tree's servers then resolve the location. Forest guides may apply local policy, so guides do not necessarily contain identical information.
sections.plainLanguage: A seeker asks for a service address, and a resolver helps find the right group of mapping servers. A forest guide identifies the tree for the area, and that tree returns the mapping.

sections.title: How Trees Resolve a Location
sections.content:
Each tree node is authoritative for a coverage region and can point to child nodes that cover smaller regions. A coverage region can be described with geographic shapes or civic address fields. A node's records either direct a query to another mapping server or provide a service URI. Leaf nodes contain service mappings; higher nodes generally direct queries to children.

In recursive operation, a node forwards the query to the matching child and returns that child's answer. In iterative operation, it returns the child's server name so the querier can continue. A node may return a region and an expiration time rather than an answer for one point, allowing the result to be cached. If regions overlap, the system can return or query all matching alternatives.
sections.plainLanguage: The first server checks which smaller area contains the location and directs the request there. The search continues until a server can return the service address, or all relevant matches if regions overlap.

sections.title: Forest Guides, Caching, and Service Numbers
sections.content:
A forest guide keeps track of tree coverage, but it does not provide the final service mapping. Trees announce coverage information to guides, and guides can exchange that information with peers. Signed coverage information is recommended so recipients can check its source and authorization. Peering requires trust between the operators, and policy can limit which coverage information a guide shares.

Seekers and resolvers may cache results, including answers for a region, to avoid repeating a lookup while the location remains within that region. The same architecture can map a location to a service number as well as a service URI. A device may need numbers valid in the user's home country and in the country being visited.
sections.plainLanguage: Forest guides keep records of which mapping trees serve each area, and lookup results can be reused until they expire. The same location-based lookup can provide a local service number as well as an Internet address.

sections.title: Security and Trust in Mapping Results
sections.content:
The architecture must address servers impersonating one another and attackers changing queries, results, or coverage regions. The RFC recommends channel security such as Transport Layer Security (TLS) to protect queries and results, and recommends digitally signing results. A signature proves which key signed data, but does not by itself prove that the signer is authorized for a geographic region.

A server that introduces a service boundary MUST sign it, and the recipient MUST use local policy to check that the signer is authorized for the region. The RFC notes that deciding which organizations may speak for a region is difficult. It also identifies denial-of-service attacks as a threat that requires operational measures.
sections.plainLanguage: A correct answer must come from a trusted server, and an authorized organization must approve each service region. Encryption and signatures help protect messages, but local rules are still needed to decide which signer controls an area.
